chunks.title: Introduction: what electrostatics studies
chunks.text: Sparks when removing a sweater, lightning and small shocks from a car door all come from charge built up by rubbing insulating surfaces and then discharging. Electrostatics is the study of forces, fields and potentials that arise from static charges, meaning charges that do not move or change with time.

chunks.title: Electric charge: two kinds, like repel and unlike attract
chunks.text: Rubbing materials together electrifies them. There are only two kinds of charge: like charges repel and unlike charges attract. The property that separates the two kinds is called the polarity of charge. By convention, the charge on a glass rod or cat's fur is called positive and the charge on a plastic rod or silk is called negative. Rubbing a glass rod with silk moves electrons from the rod to the silk; no new charge is created.

chunks.title: Conductors and insulators
chunks.text: Conductors let charge move through them easily because they contain comparatively free electrons. Metals, human and animal bodies and the earth are conductors. Most non-metals, such as glass, porcelain, plastic, nylon and wood, strongly resist the flow of charge and are called insulators. Charge given to a conductor spreads over its surface, while charge put on an insulator stays where it was placed.

chunks.title: Properties of charge: additivity and conservation
chunks.text: Charges add like real numbers (scalars): the total charge of a system is the algebraic sum of the individual charges, with signs. Charge is conserved: it cannot be created or destroyed in an isolated system, only moved from one body to another. Rubbing transfers charge; it does not create it.

chunks.title: Quantisation of charge
chunks.text: Every free charge is an integer multiple of a basic unit e, so q = n e where n is a positive or negative integer. The basic charge e is about 1.6 x 10^-19 C. At everyday (macroscopic) scales the charges are so large compared with e that quantisation can be ignored and charge treated as continuous.

chunks.title: Coulomb's law
chunks.text: The force between two point charges q1 and q2 a distance r apart is proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to r squared: F = k |q1 q2| / r^2, acting along the line joining them. In SI units k = 1/(4 pi epsilon_0), about 9 x 10^9 N m^2 C^-2, and the permittivity of free space epsilon_0 is about 8.854 x 10^-12 C^2 N^-1 m^-2. Like charges repel and unlike charges attract.

chunks.title: Forces between multiple charges: superposition
chunks.text: For several charges, the force on any one charge is the vector sum of the forces from each of the other charges, each found with Coulomb's law as if the others were absent. The presence of other charges does not change an individual pairwise force. This is the principle of superposition.

chunks.title: Electric field and the field of a system of charges
chunks.text: The electric field at a point is the force per unit positive test charge placed there, E = F/q. For a point source charge Q it has magnitude Q/(4 pi epsilon_0 r^2) and points radially away from a positive charge. The test charge must be very small so it does not disturb the source. The field of a system of charges is the vector sum of the fields of each charge (superposition).

chunks.title: Electric field lines
chunks.text: A field line is a curve whose tangent at each point gives the direction of the field there. Field lines start on positive charges and end on negative charges (or at infinity). In a charge-free region they are continuous curves without breaks. Two field lines never cross, because the field at a crossing point would have two directions. Electrostatic field lines do not form closed loops. Crowded lines mean a strong field.

chunks.title: Electric flux
chunks.text: Electric flux through a small area is the field times the area times the cosine of the angle between the field and the area's normal: d(phi) = E . dS. Total flux through a surface is the sum over all small areas. Flux measures the number of field lines crossing the surface. Its SI unit is N C^-1 m^2.

chunks.title: Electric dipole
chunks.text: An electric dipole is a pair of equal and opposite charges q and -q separated by distance 2a. Its dipole moment p has magnitude q x 2a and points from -q to +q. Far from the dipole, its field falls off as 1/r^3, faster than the 1/r^2 field of a single charge. Molecules such as water have a permanent dipole moment.

chunks.title: Dipole in a uniform external field
chunks.text: In a uniform field the net force on a dipole is zero, but the two forces act at different points, so the dipole feels a torque tau = p x E, of magnitude pE sin(theta). The torque tends to align p with E. In a non-uniform field the dipole also feels a net force, which is why a charged comb attracts small bits of paper.

chunks.title: Gauss's law
chunks.text: Gauss's law: the total electric flux through any closed surface equals the total charge enclosed by the surface divided by epsilon_0, phi = q/epsilon_0. If the surface encloses no charge, the net flux through it is zero. Charges outside the surface do not change the net flux. The law is most useful for finding fields when the charge distribution has symmetry.

chunks.title: Applications of Gauss's law: line, plane sheet, spherical shell
chunks.text: Infinitely long straight wire with linear charge density lambda: E = lambda/(2 pi epsilon_0 r), radial, outward for positive lambda. Infinite plane sheet with surface charge density sigma: E = sigma/(2 epsilon_0), normal to the sheet and independent of distance. Uniformly charged thin spherical shell: outside, the field is as if the whole charge sat at the centre; inside, the field is zero at every point.
